newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania retreats from crisis as Western envoy due.
newsitem.headline: Albania retreats from crisis as Western envoy due.

text.p: Albania stepped back from fresh turmoil on Wednesday as President Sali Berisha postponed a decree on new elections, which most political parties had said they would boycott.
Berisha made the compromise over the vote as European envoy Franz Vranitzky prepared to return to Tirana on Thursday for yet more talks on getting early elections back on track.

The elections are part of international efforts to prevent Albania, Europe's poorest nation, falling back into the chaos that engulfed it in February and March after the collapse of dubious savings schemes.
Berisha had said in the morning he would dissolve parliament and set June 29 as the election day.
But his office later said Berisha had postponed the signing of the decree calling the vote.
"The decree will be signed as soon as the conditions for parliament to be dissolved are right," Berisha's spokeswoman said. "The decree will not be for now."
The early elections were part of a package of measures agreed by Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party in March as Albania was torn apart by riots and looting.
He also agreed to share power with the Socialist Party and other groups in a nine-party Government of Reconciliation.

But Albania was pushed to the brink of a fresh crisis over the elections after the Democrats, who have a big parliamentary majority, pushed through an election law which the other eight parties in the government said favoured Berisha.
Agreement on the election law was part of a six-point political contract brokered by Vranitzky on his last visit to Albania last Friday.

The other parties were unhappy over the division of seats between proportional representation and majority voting and were furious that the law was presented to parliament by the Democrats rather than by the national unity government.
The other parties in the government said they would stand by their threat to boycott the vote if it was held under the law pushed through by the Democrats.
The Socialists pulled out of the last elections in May 1996, which international observers said were flawed.
The Democratic Party insisted its law was in line with last week's Vranitzky deal and agreements with other parties.
The Socialists said they were still ready for compromise.
"We will make attempts with political and institutional means (for compromise)," said Socialist Party chief Fatos Nano.
Socialist Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, returning from a trip to Washington, also said compromise was necessary.
"I think we have to overcome this crisis. We should talk with Vranitzky after his arrival today or tomorrow, with President Berisha and with the political parties," Fino told Albanian Television.

Another key point of the Vranitzky contract was the disbanding of so-called salvation committees, formed mostly in the south of the country at the time of the rioting to bring back order as the state administration collapsed.

The contract said they should disband 46 days before the election, but they have said they will break up only if the elections are guaranteed to be free and fair. A meeting of the committees is due on Friday.
